title: Total TypeScript Tour and AMA!
summary: Matt Pocock hosts an AMA stream (after recovering from his internet dying mid-stream) covering TypeScript philosophy, ecosystem news, and career advice, then gives a guided tour of his Total TypeScript course platform. He answers whether OOP is possible in TypeScript (yes - it is fully flexible), argues TypeScript is best learned by treating it as a way to describe JavaScript, discusses Donny's stc project rewriting TypeScript in Rust, the types-as-comments proposal for JavaScript, and why he holds a high bar for adopting new tech like signals. He demos the course's problem-solution exercise format, works through the classic partial-inference limitation (you cannot pass one generic and infer another) and its curried-function workaround, and explains his view that TypeScript wizardry is a mindset of solving other people's type problems.
what_you_learn: You get a senior developer's mental models for TypeScript: primitives before patterns, the art-critic analogy for learning types, and the partial-inference limitation with its standard workaround - knowledge that makes generic-heavy library code readable instead of magical. The exercise-format tour also shows what deliberate practice looks like for type-level programming.

skills.name: Learning & Teaching

skills.name: Spec-Driven Development

learnings.title: TypeScript is fully flexible - OOP and FP both fit
learnings.detail: Answering the mirror-image of the classic question: people thought early TypeScript was too OOP-heavy (interfaces, classes, enums), but today the complaint is you cannot do OOP because everything looks functional. Matt's answer: TypeScript supports both styles completely; he personally writes mostly function-and-hooks style because years of React shaped him, not because classes are impossible.

learnings.title: TypeScript disappears at runtime - that fact unlocks learning it
learnings.detail: The single most important fact for learners: all types are erased when the code runs. If you understand that, TypeScript becomes a way to describe JavaScript rather than a separate language, and it can even make learning JavaScript easier because it forces you to categorize what JS does intuitively.

learnings.title: The art critic analogy for learning TypeScript
learnings.detail: JavaScript is like painting intuitively - you are in the flow, unrestricted. TypeScript makes you an art critic: you must place everything you made instinctively into boxes and categories. Code that feels trivial in JS (iterating object keys to build a new object) can feel hard in TS because you now have to name and bound it.

learnings.title: Rewriting TypeScript in Rust is pioneering work with no prior art
learnings.detail: Donny (kdy1, author of swc) is rewriting the TypeScript compiler in Rust as stc. Matt interviewed him over Twitter DMs because Donny is not confident in spoken English. The goal is not to change how TypeScript works but to parallelize more work and skip some config surface to go faster - and it is exactly the kind of work where ChatGPT helps least, because LLMs shine when there is lots of prior art.

learnings.title: JavaScript will not be replaced by TypeScript - types as comments will bridge them
learnings.detail: Matt's prediction: TypeScript carries too much baggage (enums, experimental decorators) to become JavaScript. Instead the types-as-comments proposal will be accepted: it reserves syntactic space in JS files where TypeScript annotations can live, and tsc type-checks those zones - giving typed JavaScript without a new language.

learnings.title: Hold a high bar for new technology
learnings.detail: On Deno, signals (after a Ryan Carniato talk he calls one of the best he has seen - 'rendering is just a side effect'), and Solid: all cool, none adopted. His filter is pragmatic: he can still build great apps in React, and if a technology is not going to get people jobs or change what he teaches, it is not worth the switch yet.

learnings.title: Coding is turning a poorly defined spec into a well-defined one
learnings.detail: On whether ChatGPT replaces programming: no-code tools work for simple static sites, but as soon as behavior exists (a shopping cart with states and sequences) you must specify exactly what happens in every state. That act of specification IS programming - and reaching a semantic impasse with a generator still ends with you editing the code yourself.

learnings.title: Total TypeScript teaches by withholding the last step
learnings.detail: Touring totaltypescript.com: most lessons are problem-solution exercises in an embedded editor, each with a video AND a written article (tens of thousands of words). The pedagogy: give all the context needed to understand the problem, then deliberately omit the one concept needed to solve it - forcing retrieval, doc reading, and active learning. Advanced learners speed-run; stuck learners hit exactly the boundary of their knowledge.

learnings.title: Partial inference: you cannot pass one generic and infer another
learnings.detail: The makeSelectors exercise: a function taking a source plus a record of selector functions needs both TSource and TSelectors, but passing one type argument locks the other to its default ({}). TypeScript cannot partially infer. The canonical workaround: split into two chained calls - makeSelectors<TSource>()(selectors) - one generic per function, so the second infers while the first is explicit.

learnings.title: Wizardry is a mindset: solve people's problems and stay wrong-able
learnings.detail: Matt's origin story: on the xstate core team he tried to improve its types, fell down the rabbit hole, and started answering strangers' TypeScript questions publicly. The mindset that got him far: 'I can find a solution to this' plus 'I am willing to be wrong in my solution' - he posted many answers that others improved, and learned from every correction.

learnings.title: TypeScript's growth eras are over - it has plateaued into the ecosystem
learnings.detail: He traces the eras: pre-Angular, the Angular adoption spike, Ember and knockout support, JSX and framework spread - and now the era where bundlers (Vite, esbuild, swc, Turbopack) and runtimes (Deno) ship TypeScript support out of the box. When the ecosystem stops needing to be convinced, growth as a separate technology is essentially complete; the next frontier is types-as-comments in JavaScript itself.

learnings.title: Typing external APIs: infer, validate, generate, or minimize
learnings.detail: Asked how to type an enormous external object: in a full-stack TypeScript repo, infer from backend to frontend. Across a boundary, validate at the IO edge with Zod (his favorite library), or auto-generate types from an OpenAPI/Swagger spec. Last resort and often best: write an interface containing only the properties you actually care about - you might not need the rest.

key_points: TypeScript completely disappears at runtime - everything else about it follows from that.
You cannot pass one generic type argument and infer the other; curry into two function calls.
Programming is converting a poorly defined spec into a well-defined one; generators cannot do that for you.
The types-as-comments proposal, not TypeScript, is the future of typed JavaScript.
Become a wizard by solving strangers' problems in public and remaining willing to be wrong.
Learn the primitives first; patterns are just how primitives fit together.
For external APIs, type only the properties you care about.
Hold a high bar for shiny technology: cool is not a reason to switch.
